newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission warns governments on sexual harassment.
newsitem.headline: Commission warns governments on sexual harassment.

text.p: The European Commission criticised governments on Wednesday for not doing enough to fight sexual harassment in the workplace and warned that it might propose new legislation.

"Sexual harassment is an affront to the dignity of the individual and one of the most offensive and demeaning experiences an employee can be subjected to," the European Union executive said in a report.
Employers must be legally required to maintain a workplace that is free of the practice, it said.
The Commission said it wanted labour and management groups to negotiate a comprehensive EU policy against sexual harassment, but it would consider proposing legislation if it was not satisfied.

Existing national laws are often ineffective because they aim to punish severe cases of sexual harassment rather than to prevent the problem or they refer to abstract concepts such as "good behaviour".

"The existence of sexual harassment is not acknowledged under these procedures until it has already severely damaged both individuals and the company as a whole," it said. Only Belgium and the Netherlands have satisfactory laws, it said.

The Commission asked the European Trade Union Confederation, the Union of Industrial and Employers' Confederations (UNICE) and the European Centre of Enterprises with Public Participation (CEEP) to draw up new rules.

In official terms, it has launched the second stage of consulations with the "social partners" under the Social Protocol of the Maastricht Treaty. The protocol allows labour and management to negotiate accords that can be turned into EU law. Britain is exempt from the provisions.
The Commission said it wants a policy that defines sexual harassment and outlines steps companies must take to prevent it and to help and advise victims.

Sexual harassment should not be defined only as sexual blackmail, where the victim is promised job advantages, the Commission said. It should also cover cases where harassment creates a "hostile, abusive or offensive working environment", it said.
The three groups have six weeks to let the Commission know whether they are willing to negotiate.

In the first stage of consultations, opinion was divided between employer organisations, which generally wanted to build on existing national initiatives, and labour groups, which wanted a binding EU instrument, the Commission said.
